claim: Cav3.2 T-type calcium channel is a major molecular actor of neuropathic pain in peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Cav3.2 T-type calcium channel is a major molecular actor of neuropathic pain in peripheral sensory neurons, but its involvement at the supraspinal level is almost unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research on peripheral expression of Cav3.2 channels in neuropathic pain.

claim: The involvement of Cav3.2 T-type calcium channel at the supraspinal level is almost unknown.
source: Cav3.2 T-type calcium channel is a major molecular actor of neuropathic pain in peripheral sensory neurons, but its involvement at the supraspinal level is almost unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Cav3.2 channels are expressed in a subpopulation of GABAergic neurons coexpressing parvalbumin in the anterior pretectum.
source: In the anterior pretectum (APT), a hub of connectivity of the somatosensory system involved in pain perception, we show that Cav3.2 channels are expressed in a subpopulation of GABAergic neurons coexpressing parvalbumin (PV).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing co-labeling of GFP (Cav3.2) and PV, as well as scRT-PCR data showing GAD65/67 expression.

claim: The anterior pretectum is a hub of connectivity of the somatosensory system involved in pain perception.
source: In the anterior pretectum (APT), a hub of connectivity of the somatosensory system involved in pain perception, we show that Cav3.2 channels are expressed in a subpopulation of GABAergic neurons coexpressing parvalbumin (PV).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies of the APT.

claim: In PV-expressing neurons of the APT, Cav3.2 channels contribute to high-frequency-bursting activity.
source: In these PV-expressing neurons, Cav3.2 channels contribute to a high-frequency-bursting activity, which is increased in the spared nerve injury model of neuropathy.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings showing that Ni2+ (Cav3.2 blocker) reduces burst activity.

claim: High-frequency-bursting activity in PV-expressing neurons of the APT is increased in the spared nerve injury model of neuropathy.
source: In these PV-expressing neurons, Cav3.2 channels contribute to a high-frequency-bursting activity, which is increased in the spared nerve injury model of neuropathy.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings comparing sham and SNI mice, showing increased firing rate, proportion of spikes in bursts, and spike frequency within bursts.

claim: Specific deletion of Cav3.2 channels in APT neurons reduced both the initiation and maintenance of mechanical allodynia.
source: Specific deletion of Cav3.2 channels in APT neurons reduced both the initiation and maintenance of mechanical and cold allodynia.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing reduced paw withdrawal thresholds in APT-KO mice compared to control KI mice in both preventive and therapeutic paradigms.

claim: Specific deletion of Cav3.2 channels in APT neurons reduced both the initiation and maintenance of cold allodynia.
source: Specific deletion of Cav3.2 channels in APT neurons reduced both the initiation and maintenance of mechanical and cold allodynia.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing increased paw withdrawal latencies in cold water tests in APT-KO mice compared to control KI mice.

claim: Centrally expressed Cav3.2 channels play a fundamental role in pain pathophysiology.
source: These data are a direct demonstration that centrally expressed Cav3.2 channels also play a fundamental role in pain pathophysiology.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined data showing that local deletion of Cav3.2 in APT reduces neuropathic pain behaviors.

claim: The Cav3.2 isoform of T-type calcium channels is overexpressed in dorsal root ganglion neurons after chronic constrictive injury of the sciatic nerve.
source: In particular, at the peripheral level, it was shown that the Cav3.2 isoform of the low-threshold T-type calcium channels (T channels) is overexpressed in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons after chronic constrictive injury of the sciatic nerve (Jagodic et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jagodic et al., 2008.

claim: Silencing the Cav3.2 isoform using intrathecal antisense oligonucleotides administration had profound antihyperalgesic and antiallodynic effects in various neuropathic pain models.
source: Silencing the Cav3.2 isoform using intrathecal antisense oligonucleotides administration had profound antihyperalgesic and antiallodynic effects in various neuropathic pain models (Bourinet et al., 2005; Messinger et al., 2009; Takahashi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Specific knockout of Cav3.2 in a subtype of DRG neurons alleviated both mechanical and cold allodynia produced by spared nerve injury.
source: Furthermore, specific knockout (KO) of Cav3.2 in a subtype of DRG neurons alleviated both mechanical and cold allodynia produced by spared nerve injury (SNI) (François et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to François et al., 2015.

claim: In situ hybridization studies revealed strong expression of the Cav3.2 transcript in scattered neurons of the anterior pretectum.
source: In the central nervous system, in situ hybridization studies revealed strong expression of the Cav3.2 transcript in scattered neurons of the anterior pretectum (APT) (Talley et al., 1999), a crossroads of ascending and descending connectivity of the somatosensory system (Rees and Roberts, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Talley et al., 1999.

claim: The anterior pretectum is a crossroads of ascending and descending connectivity of the somatosensory system.
source: In the central nervous system, in situ hybridization studies revealed strong expression of the Cav3.2 transcript in scattered neurons of the anterior pretectum (APT) (Talley et al., 1999), a crossroads of ascending and descending connectivity of the somatosensory system (Rees and Roberts, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rees and Roberts, 1993.

claim: Brief low-intensity electrical or chemical stimulations of the APT elicited antinociception.
source: The idea that APT plays a key role in nociception dates back to the 1980s, when it was shown that brief low-intensity electrical or chemical stimulations of this nucleus elicited antinociception (Prado and Roberts, 1985; Rees and Roberts, 1993; Roberts and Rees, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies from the 1980s.

claim: Involvement of APT in chronic pain was confirmed by lesions and stimulations performed in different rodent pain models.
source: Involvement of APT in chronic pain was later confirmed by lesions and stimulations performed in different rodent pain models (Rees et al., 1995; Rossaneis et al., 2014; Rossaneis and Prado, 2015; Villarreal et al., 2004; Villarreal et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: An increase in firing of fast-bursting neurons was reported in a model of central pain syndrome.
source: To date the excitability of this structure has been little studied (Bokor et al., 2005) but an increase firing of fast-bursting neurons was reported in a model of central pain syndrome (Murray et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Murray et al., 2010.

claim: T channels are involved in burst generation in numerous neuronal populations.
source: Since T channels are involved in burst generation in numerous neuronal populations (Lambert et al., 2014), we took advantage of a murine model that allows the identification of the Cav3.2 channels and their conditional deletion in specific area (François et al., 2015) to investigate their role in shaping APT neuron excitability and the initiation and maintenance of neuropathic pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lambert et al., 2014.

claim: 20.0 ± 3.9% of the APT cells express the Cav3.2-GFP channel.
source: Co-labeling of GFP- and NeuN-positive cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showed that 20.0 ± 3.9% of the APT cells express the Cav3.2-GFP channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 87.1 ± 10.0% of Cav3.2-GFP+ cells coexpress PV.
source: We thus determined that 87.1 ± 10.0% of Cav3.2-GFP+ cells coexpress PV.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of co-labeling experiments.

claim: 91.8 ± 5.6% of PV+ cells coexpress Cav3.2-GFP.
source: Conversely 91.8 ± 5.6% of PV+ cells coexpress Cav3.2-GFP confirming the overlap between the Cav3.2-GFP+ and PV+ cell populations (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of co-labeling experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 77% of PV+ units recorded in sham mice had a peak around 2–5 ms in their autocorrelogram, indicating their ability to elicit bursts.
source: As shown in Figure 2E, 77% (n = 21) of the units had a peak around 2–5 ms in their autocorrelogram, indicating their ability to elicit bursts, and are thus referred to as 'bursting cells'.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The mean firing rate of bursting PV+ cells in sham mice was 8.4 ± 2.8 Hz.
source: Their mean firing rate was 8.4 ± 2.8 Hz and bursts, consisting of 2–3 action potentials (mean: 2.9 ± 0.6) occurring at 252 ± 18.7 Hz, represented 13.7 ± 6.8% of the total number of spikes.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of in vivo electrophysiology data.

claim: Bursts in PV+ cells of sham mice consisted of 2–3 action potentials (mean: 2.9 ± 0.6) occurring at 252 ± 18.7 Hz.
source: Their mean firing rate was 8.4 ± 2.8 Hz and bursts, consisting of 2–3 action potentials (mean: 2.9 ± 0.6) occurring at 252 ± 18.7 Hz, represented 13.7 ± 6.8% of the total number of spikes.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of in vivo electrophysiology data.

claim: Bursts represented 13.7 ± 6.8% of the total number of spikes in PV+ cells of sham mice.
source: Their mean firing rate was 8.4 ± 2.8 Hz and bursts, consisting of 2–3 action potentials (mean: 2.9 ± 0.6) occurring at 252 ± 18.7 Hz, represented 13.7 ± 6.8% of the total number of spikes.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of in vivo electrophysiology data.

claim: The mean firing rate of regular PV+ cells in sham mice was 4.4 ± 1.7 Hz.
source: The six remaining units showed a flat distribution of interspike intervals (ISIs) with a mean firing rate of 4.4 ± 1.7 Hz, and are thus referred to as 'regular cells' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of bursting cells was similar between sham (77%) and SNI (75%) animals.
source: Although the proportion of bursting cells was similar in the two conditions (77% vs. 75%, respectively), we observed a significant increase upon SNI, in the mean firing rate (Figure 2F; left panel; 11.4 ± 3.2 Hz; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.0036), in the proportion of spikes belonging to a burst (Figure 2F; middle panel; 20.9 ± 7.8%; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0039), and in the mean spike frequency within a burst (Figure 2F; right panel; 270.6 ± 20.6 Hz; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of in vivo electrophysiology data between sham and SNI mice.

claim: There was a significant increase in mean firing rate of bursting PV+ cells in SNI mice (11.4 ± 3.2 Hz) compared to sham mice (p = 0.0036).
source: Although the proportion of bursting cells was similar in the two conditions (77% vs. 75%, respectively), we observed a significant increase upon SNI, in the mean firing rate (Figure 2F; left panel; 11.4 ± 3.2 Hz; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.0036), in the proportion of spikes belonging to a burst (Figure 2F; middle panel; 20.9 ± 7.8%; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0039), and in the mean spike frequency within a burst (Figure 2F; right panel; 270.6 ± 20.6 Hz; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There was a significant increase in the proportion of spikes belonging to a burst in SNI mice (20.9 ± 7.8%) compared to sham mice (p = 0.0039).
source: Although the proportion of bursting cells was similar in the two conditions (77% vs. 75%, respectively), we observed a significant increase upon SNI, in the mean firing rate (Figure 2F; left panel; 11.4 ± 3.2 Hz; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.0036), in the proportion of spikes belonging to a burst (Figure 2F; middle panel; 20.9 ± 7.8%; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0039), and in the mean spike frequency within a burst (Figure 2F; right panel; 270.6 ± 20.6 Hz; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There was a significant increase in the mean spike frequency within a burst in SNI mice (270.6 ± 20.6 Hz) compared to sham mice (p = 0.01).
source: Although the proportion of bursting cells was similar in the two conditions (77% vs. 75%, respectively), we observed a significant increase upon SNI, in the mean firing rate (Figure 2F; left panel; 11.4 ± 3.2 Hz; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.0036), in the proportion of spikes belonging to a burst (Figure 2F; middle panel; 20.9 ± 7.8%; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0039), and in the mean spike frequency within a burst (Figure 2F; right panel; 270.6 ± 20.6 Hz; Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No difference was observed in the mean firing rates of regular cells between sham and SNI animals (p = 0.35).
source: No difference was observed in the mean firing rates of regular cells for which the mean spike frequency in SNI animals was 6.7 ± 3.9 Hz (Wilcoxon sum rank test; p = 0.35).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of in vivo electrophysiology data.

claim: Most of the PV+ and Cav3.2+ neurons of the APT are bursting neurons.
source: We therefore concluded that most of the PV+ and Cav3.2+ neurons of the APT are bursting neurons and that their bursting activities are enhanced in the neuropathic pain state.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the in vivo recording data showing 77% of PV+ neurons are bursting cells.

claim: The bursting activities of PV+ and Cav3.2+ neurons of the APT are enhanced in the neuropathic pain state.
source: We therefore concluded that most of the PV+ and Cav3.2+ neurons of the APT are bursting neurons and that their bursting activities are enhanced in the neuropathic pain state.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the in vivo recording data showing increased bursting parameters in SNI mice.

claim: All APT fluorescent PV+ neurons behaved as fast-spiking neurons with a high discharge rate (mean maximal firing rate: 214 ± 112 Hz).
source: In response to a pulse of depolarizing current all APT fluorescent neurons behaved as fast-spiking neurons with a high discharge rate (mean maximal firing rate upon depolarizing current of increasing amplitude: 214 ± 112 Hz, n = 60, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In response to hyperpolarizing current, PV+ neurons showed a large amplitude sag (17 ± 6 mV) indicating the presence of an Ih current.
source: In response to the injection of a hyperpolarizing current step (peak hyperpolarization ranging from −95 to −105 mV), common features were a large amplitude sag (17 ± 6 mV, n = 62), indicating the presence of an Ih current, and a rebound depolarization that underlie a burst of high-frequency action potentials in 57 out of 62 recorded neurons (mean number of spikes 7 ± 4, n = 57).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings.

claim: 57 out of 62 recorded PV+ neurons showed a rebound depolarization that underlie a burst of high-frequency action potentials (mean number of spikes 7 ± 4).
source: In response to the injection of a hyperpolarizing current step (peak hyperpolarization ranging from −95 to −105 mV), common features were a large amplitude sag (17 ± 6 mV, n = 62), indicating the presence of an Ih current, and a rebound depolarization that underlie a burst of high-frequency action potentials in 57 out of 62 recorded neurons (mean number of spikes 7 ± 4, n = 57).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings.

claim: All PV+ neurons expressed PV transcript.
source: All neurons expressed PV transcript and among them, 73.9% expressed GAD65 and/or GAD67 mRNA (n = 17/23), the remaining ones (n = 6/23) expressed Vglut2 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data.

claim: 73.9% of PV+ neurons expressed GAD65 and/or GAD67 mRNA.
source: All neurons expressed PV transcript and among them, 73.9% expressed GAD65 and/or GAD67 mRNA (n = 17/23), the remaining ones (n = 6/23) expressed Vglut2 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data showing 17 out of 23 neurons expressed GAD65/67.

claim: 26.1% of PV+ neurons expressed Vglut2 mRNA.
source: All neurons expressed PV transcript and among them, 73.9% expressed GAD65 and/or GAD67 mRNA (n = 17/23), the remaining ones (n = 6/23) expressed Vglut2 mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data showing 6 out of 23 neurons expressed Vglut2.

claim: The Cav3.2 transcript was present in 13 out of 17 GABAergic PV+ neurons.
source: Importantly the Cav3.2 transcript was present in 13 out of the 17 GABAergic neurons but never detected in glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data.

claim: The Cav3.2 transcript was never detected in glutamatergic PV+ neurons.
source: Importantly the Cav3.2 transcript was present in 13 out of the 17 GABAergic neurons but never detected in glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data showing 0 out of 6 glutamatergic neurons expressed Cav3.2.

claim: Cav3.1 mRNA was detected in 10 out of 13 GABAergic neurons coexpressing Cav3.2.
source: mRNA of the two other Cav3 isoforms was also detected, albeit less frequently (Cav3.1: n = 10/13; Cav3.3: n = 3/13) in GABAergic neurons coexpressing Cav3.2 and in glutamatergic neurons (Cav3.1: n = 5/6; Cav3.3: n = 1/6).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data.

claim: Cav3.3 mRNA was detected in 3 out of 13 GABAergic neurons coexpressing Cav3.2.
source: mRNA of the two other Cav3 isoforms was also detected, albeit less frequently (Cav3.1: n = 10/13; Cav3.3: n = 3/13) in GABAergic neurons coexpressing Cav3.2 and in glutamatergic neurons (Cav3.1: n = 5/6; Cav3.3: n = 1/6).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data.

claim: Cav3.1 mRNA was detected in 5 out of 6 glutamatergic PV+ neurons.
source: mRNA of the two other Cav3 isoforms was also detected, albeit less frequently (Cav3.1: n = 10/13; Cav3.3: n = 3/13) in GABAergic neurons coexpressing Cav3.2 and in glutamatergic neurons (Cav3.1: n = 5/6; Cav3.3: n = 1/6).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data.

claim: Cav3.3 mRNA was detected in 1 out of 6 glutamatergic PV+ neurons.
source: mRNA of the two other Cav3 isoforms was also detected, albeit less frequently (Cav3.1: n = 10/13; Cav3.3: n = 3/13) in GABAergic neurons coexpressing Cav3.2 and in glutamatergic neurons (Cav3.1: n = 5/6; Cav3.3: n = 1/6).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data.

claim: PV+ neurons expressing the Cav3.2 channels are fast-spiking GABAergic neurons.
source: These results strongly suggest that PV+ neurons expressing the Cav3.2 channels are fast-spiking GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined electrophysiological and transcriptomic data.

claim: Application of 100 µM Ni2+ significantly decreased the number of action potentials in rebound bursts (from 7.0 ± 3.1 to 3.8 ± 2.8; p = 0.0039).
source: As shown in Figure 4A, C, application of 100 µM Ni2+, a concentration that specifically blocks Cav3.2 channels (Lee et al., 1999), significantly decreased the number of action potentials (ctr: 7.0 ± 3.1/Ni2+: 3.8 ± 2.8; n = 8; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0039), the firing frequency (min ISI: ctr: 3.4 ± 0.9 ms/Ni2+: 6.6 ± 4.0 ms; n = 6; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0156) and the amplitude of the underlying depolarization measured in the presence of TTX (ctr: 13.6 ± 5.2/Ni2+: 10.8 ± 6.1 mV; n = 10; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0029).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: 100 µM Ni2+ is a concentration that specifically blocks Cav3.2 channels.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, C, application of 100 µM Ni2+, a concentration that specifically blocks Cav3.2 channels (Lee et al., 1999), significantly decreased the number of action potentials (ctr: 7.0 ± 3.1/Ni2+: 3.8 ± 2.8; n = 8; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0039), the firing frequency (min ISI: ctr: 3.4 ± 0.9 ms/Ni2+: 6.6 ± 4.0 ms; n = 6; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0156) and the amplitude of the underlying depolarization measured in the presence of TTX (ctr: 13.6 ± 5.2/Ni2+: 10.8 ± 6.1 mV; n = 10; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0029).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 1999.

claim: Application of 100 µM Ni2+ significantly decreased the firing frequency in rebound bursts (min ISI from 3.4 ± 0.9 ms to 6.6 ± 4.0 ms; p = 0.0156).
source: As shown in Figure 4A, C, application of 100 µM Ni2+, a concentration that specifically blocks Cav3.2 channels (Lee et al., 1999), significantly decreased the number of action potentials (ctr: 7.0 ± 3.1/Ni2+: 3.8 ± 2.8; n = 8; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0039), the firing frequency (min ISI: ctr: 3.4 ± 0.9 ms/Ni2+: 6.6 ± 4.0 ms; n = 6; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0156) and the amplitude of the underlying depolarization measured in the presence of TTX (ctr: 13.6 ± 5.2/Ni2+: 10.8 ± 6.1 mV; n = 10; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0029).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: Application of 100 µM Ni2+ significantly decreased the amplitude of the underlying depolarization measured in the presence of TTX (from 13.6 ± 5.2 to 10.8 ± 6.1 mV; p = 0.0029).
source: As shown in Figure 4A, C, application of 100 µM Ni2+, a concentration that specifically blocks Cav3.2 channels (Lee et al., 1999), significantly decreased the number of action potentials (ctr: 7.0 ± 3.1/Ni2+: 3.8 ± 2.8; n = 8; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0039), the firing frequency (min ISI: ctr: 3.4 ± 0.9 ms/Ni2+: 6.6 ± 4.0 ms; n = 6; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0156) and the amplitude of the underlying depolarization measured in the presence of TTX (ctr: 13.6 ± 5.2/Ni2+: 10.8 ± 6.1 mV; n = 10; Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 0.0029).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 4A, C.

claim: A block of all T channels isoforms using the pan antagonist TTA-P2 produced an even stronger decrease of the rebound activity than Ni2+ alone.
source: A block of all T channels isoforms using the pan antagonist TTA-P2 produced an even stronger decrease of the rebound activity, as expected from the results of the scRT-PCR (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: The distribution of the maximal number of spikes of rebound bursts evoked in PV+ neurons is shifted toward larger values in SNI compared to sham-operated mice (mean: 9.1 ± 2.3 vs. 6.3 ± 1.8; p = 0.0012).
source: As shown in Figure 4D, the distribution of the maximal number of spikes of rebound bursts evoked in PV+ neurons is shifted toward larger values in SNI compared to sham-operated mice (mean maximal number of spikes: 9.1 ± 2.3, n = 15, 6.3 ± 1.8, n = 12, for SNI and sham, respectively; Wilcoxon sum rank test p = 0.0012).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings comparing sham and SNI mice shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The difference in distribution of maximal number of spikes between SNI and sham mice is suppressed when Cav3.2 channels are blocked with 100 µM Ni2+.
source: Importantly, this difference in distribution is suppressed when Cav3.2 channels are blocked with 100 µM Ni2+, strongly suggesting that these channels participate in the increased rebound burst activities observed in SNI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings with pharmacological manipulation.

claim: Cav3.2 channels participate in the increased rebound burst activities observed in SNI mice.
source: Importantly, this difference in distribution is suppressed when Cav3.2 channels are blocked with 100 µM Ni2+, strongly suggesting that these channels participate in the increased rebound burst activities observed in SNI mice.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pharmacological data showing that Ni2+ eliminates the difference between sham and SNI mice.

claim: No significant differences were found in the PWT between baseline measurements before and 2 weeks after viral injections within each group.
source: Prior to SNI procedure, two baseline measurements were performed, before and 2 weeks after viral injections. No significant differences were found in the PWT between these two measurements within each group or between KI and APT-KO mice, indicating that neither the viral injection by itself, nor the local deletion of Cav3.2 impacts acute mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing baseline measurements.

claim: No significant differences were found in the PWT between KI and APT-KO mice at baseline.
source: Prior to SNI procedure, two baseline measurements were performed, before and 2 weeks after viral injections. No significant differences were found in the PWT between these two measurements within each group or between KI and APT-KO mice, indicating that neither the viral injection by itself, nor the local deletion of Cav3.2 impacts acute mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing baseline measurements between groups.

claim: Neither the viral injection by itself, nor the local deletion of Cav3.2 impacts acute mechanical sensitivity.
source: Prior to SNI procedure, two baseline measurements were performed, before and 2 weeks after viral injections. No significant differences were found in the PWT between these two measurements within each group or between KI and APT-KO mice, indicating that neither the viral injection by itself, nor the local deletion of Cav3.2 impacts acute mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the lack of differences in baseline measurements.

claim: A statistically significant decrease in PWT was observed in KI mice following SNI from day 14 postsurgery, confirming the development of a mechanical allodynia.
source: A statistically significant decrease in PWT was observed in KI mice following SNI from day 14 postsurgery, confirming the development of a mechanical allodynia.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing decreased PWT in KI mice after SNI.

claim: The decrease in PWT following SNI was strongly attenuated in APT-KO compared to KI mice.
source: Importantly, this decrease was strongly attenuated in APT-KO compared to KI mice (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data comparing KI and APT-KO mice shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The difference in mechanical allodynia between APT-KO mice and their KI littermates was not due to motor or coordination deficits.
source: This difference between APT-KO mice and their KI littermates was not due to motor or coordination deficits (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by rotarod and circular corridor test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: KI mice showed a decrease in withdraw latency after SNI when the operated paw was immersed in a water bath at 18°C, indicating the development of a cold allodynia.
source: While KI mice showed a decrease in withdraw latency after SNI when the operated paw was immersed in a water bath at 18°, indicating the development of a cold allodynia, this phenotype was abolished in the preventive APT-KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the paw immersion test.

claim: Cold allodynia was abolished in the preventive APT-KO mice.
source: While KI mice showed a decrease in withdraw latency after SNI when the operated paw was immersed in a water bath at 18°, indicating the development of a cold allodynia, this phenotype was abolished in the preventive APT-KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the paw immersion test comparing KI and APT-KO mice.

claim: APT-Cav3.2 channels contribute to the initiation of mechanical and cold allodynia characterizing the SNI model in both male and female mice.
source: Altogether, these results clearly indicate that APT-Cav3.2 channels contribute to the initiation of mechanical and cold allodynia characterizing the SNI model in both male and female mice.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the preventive knockout behavioral data showing reduced allodynia in both sexes.

claim: Both mechanical and cold allodynia were rapidly rescued by therapeutic KO of APT-Cav3.2.
source: Both mechanical and cold allodynia were rapidly rescued since tactile threshold lowering was drastically reduced (Figure 5C) and paw withdrawal latencies returned to preoperative baseline values (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the therapeutic knockout paradigm shown in Figure 5C and 5E.

claim: Tactile threshold lowering was drastically reduced by therapeutic KO of APT-Cav3.2.
source: Both mechanical and cold allodynia were rapidly rescued since tactile threshold lowering was drastically reduced (Figure 5C) and paw withdrawal latencies returned to preoperative baseline values (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Paw withdrawal latencies returned to preoperative baseline values by therapeutic KO of APT-Cav3.2.
source: Both mechanical and cold allodynia were rapidly rescued since tactile threshold lowering was drastically reduced (Figure 5C) and paw withdrawal latencies returned to preoperative baseline values (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Cav3.2 expressed in the APT is not only involved in the initiation but also in the maintenance of neuropathic phenotype in the SNI model.
source: Altogether, these results show that Cav3.2 expressed in the APT is not only involved in the initiation but also in the maintenance of neuropathic phenotype in the SNI model.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from both preventive and therapeutic knockout behavioral data.

claim: Deletion of Cav3.2 channels expressed in a GABAergic and PV-expressing subpopulation of APT neurons leads to an antiallodynic effect in the SNI neuropathic pain model.
source: We showed that deletion of Cav3.2 channels expressed in a GABAergic and PV-expressing subpopulation of APT neurons leads to an antiallodynic effect in the SNI neuropathic pain model.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined behavioral, electrophysiological, and molecular data.

claim: 92% of APT-PV+ neurons are able to discharge bursts of action potentials at high frequency underpinned by a rebound large transient depolarization due to the activation of T channels.
source: Our in vitro data indicate that 92% of APT-PV+ neurons are able to discharge bursts of action potentials at high frequency underpinned by a rebound large transient depolarization due to the activation of T channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings showing 57 out of 62 neurons (92%) exhibited rebound bursts.

claim: Little evidence exists for the involvement of the Cav3.2 isoform in burst generation in the central nervous system.
source: In contrast to the well-recognized role played by the Cav3.1 and 3.3 isoforms of the T channels (Kim et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2016), little evidences exist for the involvement of the Cav3.2 isoform in burst generation in the central nervous system (Candelas et al., 2019; Dumenieu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Cav3.1 and 3.3 isoforms of the T channels play a well-recognized role in burst generation.
source: In contrast to the well-recognized role played by the Cav3.1 and 3.3 isoforms of the T channels (Kim et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2016), little evidences exist for the involvement of the Cav3.2 isoform in burst generation in the central nervous system (Candelas et al., 2019; Dumenieu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The specific blockade of Cav3.2 greatly reduced the amplitude of the depolarization underlying burst generation.
source: Here, the specific blockade of this isoform greatly reduced the amplitude of the depolarization underlying burst generation and decreased the number and frequency of action potentials within a burst.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings with Ni2+ application.

claim: The specific blockade of Cav3.2 decreased the number and frequency of action potentials within a burst.
source: Here, the specific blockade of this isoform greatly reduced the amplitude of the depolarization underlying burst generation and decreased the number and frequency of action potentials within a burst.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro patch-clamp recordings with Ni2+ application.

claim: APT-PV+ GABAergic neurons express multiple isoforms of the T channels.
source: Therefore, although our transcriptomic and pharmacological results suggest that APT-PV+ GABAergic neurons express multiple isoforms of the T channels, we demonstrate that the Cav3.2 isoform has an essential contribution to the bursting behavior in this subpopulation of APT neurons and its increase in SNI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRT-PCR data showing expression of Cav3.1, Cav3.2, and Cav3.3.

claim: The Cav3.2 isoform has an essential contribution to the bursting behavior in APT-PV+ neurons.
source: Therefore, although our transcriptomic and pharmacological results suggest that APT-PV+ GABAergic neurons express multiple isoforms of the T channels, we demonstrate that the Cav3.2 isoform has an essential contribution to the bursting behavior in this subpopulation of APT neurons and its increase in SNI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data showing that Ni2+ (Cav3.2 blocker) significantly reduces burst activity.

claim: The Cav3.2 isoform has an essential contribution to the increase in bursting behavior in APT-PV+ neurons in SNI mice.
source: Therefore, although our transcriptomic and pharmacological results suggest that APT-PV+ GABAergic neurons express multiple isoforms of the T channels, we demonstrate that the Cav3.2 isoform has an essential contribution to the bursting behavior in this subpopulation of APT neurons and its increase in SNI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data showing that Ni2+ eliminates the difference in burst activity between sham and SNI mice.

claim: About 25% of rat APT neurons present high-frequency discharges.
source: Bokor et al., 2005 reported a heterogeneous firing pattern in rat APT neurons with about 25% of them presenting high-frequency discharges.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bokor et al., 2005.

claim: Fast-bursting neurons in rat APT were described as strongly expressing PV.
source: Although tested on only three neurons, these fast-bursting neurons were described as strongly expressing PV.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bokor et al., 2005.

claim: 77% of APT-PV+ neurons discharge in bursts.
source: The use of the PINP method allowed us to perform such specific characterization and our in vivo recordings of APT-PV+ neurons showed that 77% of these neurons discharge in bursts with a clear enhancement of bursting activity in SNI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data.

claim: There is a clear enhancement of bursting activity in APT-PV+ neurons in SNI mice.
source: The use of the PINP method allowed us to perform such specific characterization and our in vivo recordings of APT-PV+ neurons showed that 77% of these neurons discharge in bursts with a clear enhancement of bursting activity in SNI mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data comparing sham and SNI mice.

claim: An increased firing rate of APT neurons with a higher percentage of neurons exhibiting at least one burst was reported in spinal-lesioned rats compared with sham-operated controls.
source: Investigating changes in neuronal spiking activity in spinal-lesioned rats, Murray et al., 2010 also described an increased firing rate of APT neurons with a higher percentage of neurons exhibiting at least one burst compared with sham-operated controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Murray et al., 2010.

claim: The increase in bursting behavior in APT-PV+ neurons in SNI mice was more pronounced than in Murray et al., 2010.
source: The increase in bursting behavior reported here was more pronounced than in Murray et al., 2010 as not only the number of bursts but also the number of spikes and their frequency were enhanced indicating a profound change in this class of APT neurons in neuropathic condition.
evidence: This comparison is based on the current study's data showing increases in multiple burst parameters versus the prior study.

claim: The disparity in bursting behavior changes between the current study and Murray et al., 2010 likely stems from the ability to record an identified subpopulation of APT neurons.
source: This disparity likely stems from our ability to record an identified subpopulation of APT neurons, although a difference between neuropathic models cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: Modifications of high-frequency-bursting activities in pain condition have been reported in human and various experimental models, particularly in the thalamocortical system.
source: When considering other brain structures, modifications of high-frequency-bursting activities in pain condition have been reported in human, as well as in various experimental models, and this is particularly well documented in the thalamocortical system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In awake patients with neurogenic pain, recordings from thalamic neurons show an increase in the occurrence of high-frequency bursts.
source: In awake patients with neurogenic pain, recordings from thalamic neurons show an increase in the occurrence of high-frequency bursts (Jeanmonod et al., 1996; Lenz et al., 1989; Llinás et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Higher proportions of bursting neurons have been reported in ventralis postero-lateralis thalamic neurons following contusive spinal cord lesions in rats.
source: Similar higher proportions of bursting neurons have been reported in ventralis postero-lateralis thalamic neurons following contusive spinal cord lesions in rats (Gerke et al., 2003) and monkeys (Weng et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Higher proportions of bursting neurons have been reported in ventralis postero-lateralis thalamic neurons following contusive spinal cord lesions in monkeys.
source: Similar higher proportions of bursting neurons have been reported in ventralis postero-lateralis thalamic neurons following contusive spinal cord lesions in rats (Gerke et al., 2003) and monkeys (Weng et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: An increase in the frequency of T-channel-dependent bursts was reported in ventralis postero-lateralis thalamic neurons following induction of visceral pain in mice.
source: Furthermore, in the same thalamic nucleus, an increase in the frequency of T-channel-dependent bursts was reported following induction of visceral pain in mice (Kim et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2003.

claim: Removing Cav3.2 specifically from APT-PV+ neurons strongly reduced mechanical allodynia evoked by SNI.
source: Our behavioral analysis firstly showed that removing Cav3.2 specifically from APT-PV+ neurons strongly reduced mechanical and cold allodynia evoked by SNI.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the preventive knockout paradigm.

claim: Removing Cav3.2 specifically from APT-PV+ neurons strongly reduced cold allodynia evoked by SNI.
source: Our behavioral analysis firstly showed that removing Cav3.2 specifically from APT-PV+ neurons strongly reduced mechanical and cold allodynia evoked by SNI.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the preventive knockout paradigm.

claim: Removing the Cav3.2 channels when the SNI effects were fully developed rescues the different allodynic symptoms.
source: Furthermore, removing the Cav3.2 channels when the SNI effects were fully developed rescues the different allodynic symptoms indicating that Cav3.2 channels not only contribute to the development but also to the maintenance of the pain phenotype and strongly suggests their direct electrogenic implication in sustaining allodynia.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the therapeutic knockout paradigm.

claim: Cav3.2 channels not only contribute to the development but also to the maintenance of the pain phenotype.
source: Furthermore, removing the Cav3.2 channels when the SNI effects were fully developed rescues the different allodynic symptoms indicating that Cav3.2 channels not only contribute to the development but also to the maintenance of the pain phenotype and strongly suggests their direct electrogenic implication in sustaining allodynia.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the therapeutic knockout behavioral data.

claim: Cav3.2 channels have a direct electrogenic implication in sustaining allodynia.
source: Furthermore, removing the Cav3.2 channels when the SNI effects were fully developed rescues the different allodynic symptoms indicating that Cav3.2 channels not only contribute to the development but also to the maintenance of the pain phenotype and strongly suggests their direct electrogenic implication in sustaining allodynia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the therapeutic knockout data.

claim: The Cav3.2-dependent modification in APT-PV+ neurons activities sustaining allodynia is not sex specific.
source: Since these effects were observed on both male and female mice, the Cav3.2-dependent modification in APT-PV+ neurons activities sustaining allodynia is not sex specific, unlike what was recently reported for layer five PV+ neurons in the prelimbic region of the medial prefrontal cortex using the same neuropathic model (Jones and Sheets, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing similar effects in both male and female mice.

claim: Layer five PV+ neurons in the prelimbic region of the medial prefrontal cortex show sex-specific effects in the SNI neuropathic model.
source: Since these effects were observed on both male and female mice, the Cav3.2-dependent modification in APT-PV+ neurons activities sustaining allodynia is not sex specific, unlike what was recently reported for layer five PV+ neurons in the prelimbic region of the medial prefrontal cortex using the same neuropathic model (Jones and Sheets, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jones and Sheets, 2020.

claim: The lack of sex specificity in Cav3.2-dependent effects suggests that this mechanism is a fundamental component of chronic pain processes.
source: Such lack of sex specificity suggests that this mechanism is a fundamental component of chronic pain processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of similar effects in both sexes.

claim: Global Cav3.2−/− mice showed reduced sensitivity to acute pain but no change in the overall development of neuropathic pain compared to wild-type mice.
source: Comparing the pain phenotypes of wild-type and global Cav3.2−/− mice, Choi et al., 2007 reported reduced sensitivity to acute pain in KO mice but no change in the overall development of neuropathic pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2007.

claim: Multiple data point toward Cav3.2 as a main actor in acute and chronic pain at the peripheral level.
source: However, at the peripheral level, multiple data point toward Cav3.2 as a main actor in acute and chronic pain (Bourinet et al., 2016; Bourinet et al., 2005; François et al., 2015; Jagodic et al., 2008; Messinger et al., 2009; Takahashi et al., 2010) suggesting a possible compensatory phenomenon in condition of complete channel deletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A possible compensatory phenomenon may occur in condition of complete Cav3.2 channel deletion.
source: However, at the peripheral level, multiple data point toward Cav3.2 as a main actor in acute and chronic pain (Bourinet et al., 2016; Bourinet et al., 2005; François et al., 2015; Jagodic et al., 2008; Messinger et al., 2009; Takahashi et al., 2010) suggesting a possible compensatory phenomenon in condition of complete channel deletion.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy between global knockout and conditional knockout results.

claim: An increase in Cav3.2 mRNA was observed in the anterior cingulate cortex in the chronic constriction injury model.
source: At the supraspinal levels, very little is known. In the chronic constriction injury model, an increase in Cav3.2 mRNA was observed in the anterior cingulate cortex and local injection of NNC 55-0396, a poorly selective T-channel antagonist (Huang et al., 2004; Schäfer et al., 2016), partially relieved allodynia (Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2015.

claim: Local injection of NNC 55-0396 in the anterior cingulate cortex partially relieved allodynia in the chronic constriction injury model.
source: At the supraspinal levels, very little is known. In the chronic constriction injury model, an increase in Cav3.2 mRNA was observed in the anterior cingulate cortex and local injection of NNC 55-0396, a poorly selective T-channel antagonist (Huang et al., 2004; Schäfer et al., 2016), partially relieved allodynia (Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2015.

claim: NNC 55-0396 is a poorly selective T-channel antagonist.
source: At the supraspinal levels, very little is known. In the chronic constriction injury model, an increase in Cav3.2 mRNA was observed in the anterior cingulate cortex and local injection of NNC 55-0396, a poorly selective T-channel antagonist (Huang et al., 2004; Schäfer et al., 2016), partially relieved allodynia (Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2004 and Schäfer et al., 2016.

claim: A T-channel-dependent activation of ERK in the paraventricular thalamus following acid-induced chronic muscle pain was abolished in Cav3.2−/− mice.
source: Using various poorly specific T-channel antagonists, Chen et al., 2010 showed a T-channel-dependent activation of ERK in the paraventricular thalamus following acid-induced chronic muscle pain that was abolished in Cav3.2−/− mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of TTA-A2 induced analgesia blunting the effect of paracetamol.
source: Furthermore, intracerebroventricular injection of the specific antagonist of the three T-channel isotypes, TTA-A2, induced analgesia blunting the effect of paracetamol, the most widely used remedy to treat mild pain, an effect also abolished in Cav3.2−/− mice (Kerckhove et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kerckhove et al., 2014.

claim: The analgesic effect of intracerebroventricular TTA-A2 was abolished in Cav3.2−/− mice.
source: Furthermore, intracerebroventricular injection of the specific antagonist of the three T-channel isotypes, TTA-A2, induced analgesia blunting the effect of paracetamol, the most widely used remedy to treat mild pain, an effect also abolished in Cav3.2−/− mice (Kerckhove et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kerckhove et al., 2014.

claim: TTA-A2 is a specific antagonist of the three T-channel isotypes.
source: Furthermore, intracerebroventricular injection of the specific antagonist of the three T-channel isotypes, TTA-A2, induced analgesia blunting the effect of paracetamol, the most widely used remedy to treat mild pain, an effect also abolished in Cav3.2−/− mice (Kerckhove et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kerckhove et al., 2014.

claim: Prior experiments only suggested a central pronociceptive role of Cav3.2 channels.
source: However, such experiments only suggested a central pronociceptive role of Cav3.2 channels.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior research as being suggestive rather than definitive.

claim: Local deletion of Cav3.2 channels in 20% of the APT neurons drastically reduced allodynia.
source: Our results, showing that local deletion of Cav3.2 channels in 20% of the APT neurons drastically reduced allodynia, provide direct evidence of the involvement of central Cav3.2 channels in neuropathic pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data from the knockout experiments.

claim: The results provide direct evidence of the involvement of central Cav3.2 channels in neuropathic pain.
source: Our results, showing that local deletion of Cav3.2 channels in 20% of the APT neurons drastically reduced allodynia, provide direct evidence of the involvement of central Cav3.2 channels in neuropathic pain.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined behavioral and molecular data.

claim: APT-PV+ neurons project to the high-order somatosensory thalamic nucleus, posterior nucleus (PO).
source: Functionally, as APT-PV+ neurons project to the high-order somatosensory thalamic nucleus, posterior nucleus (PO) (Bokor et al., 2005; Giber et al., 2008), this antiallodynic effect could be a consequence of the direct involvement of this neuronal population in processing nociceptive afferents from the periphery.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bokor et al., 2005 and Giber et al., 2008.

claim: The antiallodynic effect could be a consequence of the direct involvement of APT-PV+ neurons in processing nociceptive afferents from the periphery.
source: Functionally, as APT-PV+ neurons project to the high-order somatosensory thalamic nucleus, posterior nucleus (PO) (Bokor et al., 2005; Giber et al., 2008), this antiallodynic effect could be a consequence of the direct involvement of this neuronal population in processing nociceptive afferents from the periphery.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed antiallodynic effect.

claim: The net effect of the increased bursting activity of APT-PV+ GABAergic neurons on the PO activity under neuropathic conditions is difficult to predict.
source: However, the net effect of the increased bursting activity of APT-PV+ GABAergic neurons on the PO activity under neuropathic conditions is difficult to predict.
evidence: This acknowledges the complexity of predicting circuit-level effects.

claim: APT PV+ neurons account for only a small percentage of GABAergic projections impinging on zona incerta (ZI).
source: Although they account for only a small percentage of GABAergic projections impinging on zona incerta (ZI) (Giber et al., 2008), APT PV+ neurons project to the ZI, which in turn inhibit thalamic neurons (Barthó et al., 2002; Lavallée et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Giber et al., 2008.

claim: APT PV+ neurons project to the ZI, which in turn inhibit thalamic neurons.
source: Although they account for only a small percentage of GABAergic projections impinging on zona incerta (ZI) (Giber et al., 2008), APT PV+ neurons project to the ZI, which in turn inhibit thalamic neurons (Barthó et al., 2002; Lavallée et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barthó et al., 2002 and Lavallée et al., 2005.

claim: The increased bursting activity of APT PV+ neurons may mediate disinhibition of PO neurons by silencing their ZI targets.
source: Their increased bursting activity may therefore mediate disinhibition of PO neurons by silencing their ZI targets, while conversely mediating direct monosynaptic inhibition of PO neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of potential circuit mechanisms.

claim: The increased bursting activity of APT PV+ neurons may mediate direct monosynaptic inhibition of PO neurons.
source: Their increased bursting activity may therefore mediate disinhibition of PO neurons by silencing their ZI targets, while conversely mediating direct monosynaptic inhibition of PO neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of potential circuit mechanisms.

claim: The impact of inhibitory input on thalamic neurons may result in a change in firing mode rather than in a clear decrease in firing.
source: Functionally, however, these two effects may not be opposed, as the impact of inhibitory input on thalamic neurons may result in a change in firing mode rather than in a clear decrease in firing.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of thalamic neuron physiology.

claim: PO neurons highly express Cav3.1 T channels.
source: Indeed, PO neurons, which highly express Cav3.1 T channels (Talley et al., 1999), are prone to generate rebound burst firing after transient hyperpolarization due to strong IPSP bursts originating from the APT neurons as shown in vitro by Bokor et al., 2005.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Talley et al., 1999.

claim: PO neurons are prone to generate rebound burst firing after transient hyperpolarization due to strong IPSP bursts originating from the APT neurons.
source: Indeed, PO neurons, which highly express Cav3.1 T channels (Talley et al., 1999), are prone to generate rebound burst firing after transient hyperpolarization due to strong IPSP bursts originating from the APT neurons as shown in vitro by Bokor et al., 2005.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bokor et al., 2005.

claim: Masri et al., 2009 reported an increase in firing of the PO neurons but no change in their bursting activity in spinal-lesioned rats.
source: However, Masri et al., 2009 reported an increase in firing of the PO neurons but no change in their bursting activity in spinal-lesioned rats, but the recordings were restricted to a localized area of PO containing neurons that receive convergent inputs from both hind paw and vibrissae pad.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Masri et al., 2009.

claim: The recordings in Masri et al., 2009 were restricted to a localized area of PO containing neurons that receive convergent inputs from both hind paw and vibrissae pad.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Masri et al., 2009.

claim: Determining the net effect of PV+ APT neuron activity on the thalamic neurons will require further in vivo recordings performed in their specific projection area.
source: Therefore, given the potential functional and anatomical regionalization of the PO (El-Boustani et al., 2020), determining the net effect of PV+ APT neuron activity on the thalamic neurons will required further in vivo recordings performed in their specific projection area.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: There is potential functional and anatomical regionalization of the PO.
source: Therefore, given the potential functional and anatomical regionalization of the PO (El-Boustani et al., 2020), determining the net effect of PV+ APT neuron activity on the thalamic neurons will required further in vivo recordings performed in their specific projection area.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to El-Boustani et al., 2020.

claim: Anatomical and functional investigation of the APT described descending pathways impinging through complex routes on various spinal cord neuronal types and involved in pain processing.
source: Finally, anatomical and functional investigation of the APT described descending pathways impinging through complex routes on various spinal cord neuronal types and involved in pain processing (Genaro et al., 2019; Rees and Roberts, 1993; Terenzi et al., 1992; Terenzi et al., 1991; Villarreal et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: It remains to be determined whether the PV+ neurons of the APT may participate to descending pathways and modulate nociception at the spinal level.
source: So far, it remains to be determined whether the PV+ neurons of the APT may participate to these descending pathways and modulate nociception at the spinal level.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge.

claim: The data point to Cav3.2 channels as a prime target for developing innovative analgesic pharmacology that will act at both peripheral and central levels.
source: In conclusion, our data point to Cav3.2 channels as a prime target for developing innovative analgesic pharmacology that will not only act at the peripheral level but also in central structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data showing central and peripheral roles of Cav3.2.

claim: The data highlight the need to study the functional expression of channels in specific neuronal population to decipher the complex pain processing that occurs in the central nervous system.
source: Furthermore, they highlight the need to study the functional expression of channels in specific neuronal population to decipher the complex pain processing that occurs in the central nervous system.
